paragraphs: Barlow Twins learns image representations without labels by comparing two distorted versions of the same image. The challenge is to make their representations agree without letting the network produce the same constant output for every image. Such a constant solution would satisfy agreement while discarding the information that makes the representation useful.

The method measures cross-correlations between the outputs of two identical networks and pushes the resulting matrix toward the identity matrix. This encourages corresponding representation components to agree across views while reducing overlap in the information carried by different components. The objective therefore combines consistency under image distortion with reduced redundancy inside the representation.

The abstract reports that the method needs neither large batches nor asymmetric mechanisms such as stopped gradients or a separate predictor, and benefits from very large output representations. It improves on previous methods for ImageNet semi-supervised classification with little labeled data, while matching leading performance for linear classification and transfer to classification and object detection.
icml-2021-barlow-twins-self-supervised-l.tldr: Barlow Twins learns useful image representations by making distorted views agree while reducing redundancy between representation components.

paragraphs: This paper replaces fixed attention weights with a probabilistic model of attention. Most attention networks deterministically decide how much weight to assign to different inputs. The authors investigate stochastic attention, where those weights have distributions, while addressing the optimization difficulties and complicated designs that have made this approach less common.

Their Bayesian attention belief network models unnormalized attention weights through a hierarchy of gamma distributions. A corresponding encoder uses stacked Weibull distributions to approximate the posterior, combining a deterministic upward computation with a stochastic downward computation. This construction supports differentiable optimization through a variational lower bound. The authors also describe conversion of existing deterministic attention models, including pretrained models.

On the language understanding tasks studied, the method improves over deterministic attention and leading stochastic attention approaches in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, cross-domain generalization, and resistance to adversarial attacks. Additional experiments on translation and visual question answering demonstrate applicability beyond language understanding. These findings support probabilistic attention as a practical modeling choice across several attention-based tasks.
icml-2021-bayesian-attention-belief-netw.tldr: Bayesian attention belief networks make attention probabilistic through a trainable distribution hierarchy, improving several reported measures across attention-based tasks.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether the internal structure of a deep network can help it generalize when the data distribution changes. Its concern is spurious correlation: a model may rely on associations present in its training data that do not remain useful elsewhere. The authors examine whether better behavior is already present within parts of such a model.

Using functional modular probing, they analyze subnetworks under out-of-distribution conditions. They demonstrate that models biased toward spurious correlations can still contain unbiased functional subnetworks. This motivates their functional lottery ticket hypothesis: a full network contains a suitably structured subnetwork capable of better out-of-distribution performance. The emphasis is on which functional structure is selected within the larger model.

To make that observation actionable, the authors propose Modular Risk Minimization, which learns a functional structure from a supplied dataset and addresses subnetwork selection. The method can be combined with other out-of-distribution regularization approaches. Experiments across several generalization tasks support its effectiveness, connecting the structural analysis to a practical learning procedure.
icml-2021-can-subnetwork-structure-be-th.tldr: Modular Risk Minimization selects functional subnetworks that can generalize better beyond the training distribution, even within models biased toward spurious correlations.

paragraphs: DORO addresses learning when the test population is a subpopulation of the training population. Distributionally robust optimization, or DRO, has been proposed for this setting, but the authors find that it can perform poorly and behave unstably on real, large-scale tasks. They identify sensitivity to outliers as one direct cause of these problems.

The proposed framework changes the risk function used for optimization so that robustness does not lead the model to overfit potential outliers. This joins two concerns within one objective: handling changes in the population being evaluated and limiting the influence of unusual observations. The authors develop the framework for a family of divergence measures, with particular attention to CVaR and chi-squared DRO.

The paper supplies theoretical support for the method and experiments on large modern datasets. Those experiments show improved performance and stability compared with DRO. The central finding is that addressing outlier sensitivity can make distributional robustness more effective in the studied subpopulation-shift settings, rather than treating the two robustness problems independently.
icml-2021-doro-distributional-and-outlie.tldr: DORO refines distributionally robust optimization to reduce overfitting to potential outliers, improving reported performance and stability under subpopulation shift.

paragraphs: DouZero tackles DouDizhu, a three-player card game involving both competition and collaboration. Players have incomplete information, the space of game situations is large, and the available actions can change substantially from one turn to the next. That last feature makes the game difficult for reinforcement learning methods designed around small, simple action spaces.

The system combines traditional Monte Carlo methods with deep neural networks, an encoding of actions, and parallel actors. Through self-play, this combination brings a classic learning approach to a setting with a particularly complicated set of possible moves. The contribution is a conceptually simple system showing that these ingredients can work effectively together in a demanding game.

Starting from scratch on one server with four GPUs, DouZero surpassed the existing DouDizhu programs described in the abstract after days of training. It also ranked first among 344 agents on the Botzone leaderboard. These results demonstrate strong performance in this domain and support revisiting Monte Carlo methods for problems whose action spaces challenge modern reinforcement learning algorithms.
icml-2021-douzero-mastering-doudizhu-wit.tldr: DouZero combines Monte Carlo learning, neural networks, action encoding, and parallel self-play to achieve leading reported performance in DouDizhu.

paragraphs: The lottery ticket hypothesis concerns sparse subnetworks that can be trained separately from random initialization to match the accuracy of their dense parent networks. Finding these subnetworks can be expensive because it involves repeated training, pruning, and retraining. This paper investigates whether the search can use a carefully chosen subset of training examples.

The authors introduce a Pruning-Aware Critical set, or PrAC set. Its motivation comes from examples that are difficult for a network to memorize during training or easy for it to forget during pruning. They hypothesize that these examples capture especially challenging and informative parts of the dataset, making them useful for discovering a strong sparse subnetwork.

Experiments across datasets and architectures show that training and pruning on compact PrAC sets can find competitive winning tickets while substantially reducing training iterations. The authors also demonstrate that a selected set can be reused across different network architectures. That reuse matters because the effort of identifying the subset can be shared across multiple searches.
icml-2021-efficient-lottery-ticket-findi.tldr: Carefully selected training subsets can reduce the work of finding competitive sparse subnetworks and can be reused across architectures.

paragraphs: Batch reinforcement learning uses previously collected data without further exploration. The paper studies two central tasks in that setting: finding a nearly optimal policy and estimating the value of a specified policy. It asks how difficult these tasks can remain even when the learning algorithm receives unusually favorable information.

The authors establish exponential information-theoretic lower bounds for discounted, infinite-horizon Markov decision processes with linear representations of action values. Their bounds persist when realizability holds, meaning the representation can express the relevant action-value function. They also persist with exact reward and transition information in the batch observations and with the best data distribution chosen in advance for the problem class.

A new framework combining an oracle with a batch algorithm allows the lower-bound argument to cover every data distribution. The resulting separation shows that batch learning can be exponentially harder than online learning in the analyzed setting. This is a statement about fundamental information requirements, so improving the optimization procedure alone cannot eliminate the demonstrated difficulty.
icml-2021-exponential-lower-bounds-for-b.tldr: The paper proves that batch reinforcement learning can require exponentially more information than online learning, even under favorable representation and data conditions.

paragraphs: Federated learning coordinates learning across devices, but standard algorithms such as FedAvg are mainly designed for smooth objectives without constraints. This paper studies objectives that also contain a nonsmooth regularizer. Such objectives arise when applications require properties including sparsity, low rank, monotonicity, or more general constraints on the learned solution.

The authors show that straightforward adaptations of primal methods such as FedAvg can converge poorly in this setting. They call the underlying issue the curse of primal averaging. This identifies an obstacle in the way local learning results are combined, making a simple extension of the standard federated procedure unsuitable for the composite optimization problems studied.

Their solution is Federated Dual Averaging, a primal-dual algorithm with a new server-side dual averaging procedure. That procedure is designed to avoid the identified averaging problem. Both theoretical analysis and empirical experiments show improvements over the compared baselines. The contribution therefore expands the optimization machinery available for federated applications whose objectives include nonsmooth structure.
icml-2021-federated-composite-optimizati.tldr: FedDualAvg uses server-side dual averaging to improve federated optimization with nonsmooth regularizers and constraints.

paragraphs: This paper studies federated training that directly maximizes area under the ROC curve, or AUC, an objective of interest for classification with imbalanced data. The difficulty is that the objective cannot be separated into independent contributions from individual examples. Standard federated methods built for such separable objectives therefore do not directly resolve the problem.

The authors develop algorithms for heterogeneous data by solving a distributed min-max formulation that is nonconvex in the minimizing variables and strongly concave in the maximizing variables. Their approach also applies to a broader class of problems with that structure. The main theoretical result is a communication complexity bound that is constant with respect to both the number of machines and the requested accuracy.

Experiments on benchmark datasets and chest X-rays from different organizations demonstrate the method's effectiveness. In the reported medical experiment, federated training with data from multiple hospitals improves test AUC at an individual hospital. This connects the communication result to a setting where participating organizations contribute different data.
icml-2021-federated-deep-auc-maximizatio.tldr: The proposed federated AUC algorithms handle heterogeneous data with communication complexity independent of machine count and target accuracy.

paragraphs: Model extraction attempts to reproduce a model by querying its prediction API. Learning-based attacks train a replica on the target's outputs, while algebraic attacks exploit mathematical structure to reduce the required queries. This paper extends algebraic and combined algebraic-and-learning approaches to large natural language models in a specific grey-box setting.

The target consists of a publicly available pretrained encoder followed by one private classification layer. When the encoder remains frozen, the authors find that a high-fidelity replica can be obtained with a small number of queries drawn from the normal input distribution. Because these queries resemble ordinary use, the reported attack does not depend on conspicuously unusual inputs.

When the encoder has been fine-tuned, the authors combine algebraic techniques with learning-based extraction. This hybrid improves over the learning-based state of the art without increasing the number of queries. Together, the findings show how knowledge of a public encoder can materially change extraction possibilities, with different approaches suited to frozen and fine-tuned encoders.
icml-2021-grey-box-extraction-of-natural.tldr: Public encoder knowledge enables efficient extraction of language classifiers, with algebraic attacks for frozen encoders and hybrid attacks for fine-tuned ones.

paragraphs: Training large neural networks with differentially private stochastic gradient descent creates two difficulties: storing gradients for individual examples consumes substantial memory, and privacy noise becomes problematic in high dimensions. This paper introduces a different parameterization intended to reduce both burdens while retaining the original forward and backward computation.

Each weight matrix is represented using two small gradient-carrier matrices and a residual weight matrix. This allows projected gradients to be calculated without constructing the full gradients. Reparametrized gradient perturbation adds noise to the carrier gradients and then reconstructs an update for the original weights. Historical updates guide the choice of carrier matrices; their optimality is justified for linear regression and examined empirically in deep learning.

The reported method reduces memory requirements and improves utility. For BERT, the authors report average accuracy of 83.9% across four downstream tasks at a privacy parameter of epsilon equal to 8, describing the loss relative to non-private training as within 5%. The result demonstrates a practical route to private training of a large language model.
icml-2021-large-scale-private-learning-v.tldr: Low-dimensional gradient carriers reduce the memory and utility costs of differentially private training for large neural networks.

paragraphs: Learning a binary decision tree involves both discrete choices and continuous parameters. Discrete choices determine traversal and pruning, while continuous parameters define splits and predictions. This paper proposes learning these parts together, so the tree's structure and its numerical parameters can be optimized for the same downstream task.

The authors formulate the discrete decisions through a mixed-integer program and introduce a sparse relaxation that permits gradients to pass through its solution. Argmin differentiation then connects that optimization problem to the continuous parameters. Customized forward and backward algorithms make the procedure efficient enough to serve as an implicit layer inside deep networks and to work with arbitrary loss functions.

Experiments show competitive binary trees against the single-tree and ensemble approaches tested, in both supervised and unsupervised settings. Training is faster than all compared tree-learning baselines except greedy methods, whose accuracies are not competitive in those comparisons. The result combines flexibility in how trees are trained with evidence of useful accuracy and training efficiency.
icml-2021-learning-binary-decision-trees.tldr: Argmin differentiation lets binary trees learn discrete structure and continuous parameters together and function as trainable layers in deep networks.

paragraphs: This paper studies class-conditional label noise, where the probability of replacing a true label with another label depends on those two classes. Earlier multiclass approaches corrected the training loss to account for this corruption. The authors show that noise correction can instead be moved to the final prediction step.

The proposed approach first estimates class probabilities from noisy examples using an ordinary training procedure, such as multiclass logistic regression. It then applies the correction when making predictions, allowing existing training implementations to remain unchanged. The approach supports general multiclass loss matrices, including standard classification error and losses suited to ordinal regression.

A regret transfer bound connects prediction quality on the true distribution to the quality of probability estimation on the noisy distribution. The bound suggests that learning requires more samples as the noise matrix approaches singularity. The authors also extend a property of binary probability-estimation losses to multiple classes and propose fixes and possible improvements to anchor-point noise estimation. Their experiments support the theoretical findings.
icml-2021-learning-from-noisy-labels-wit.tldr: Under class-conditional label noise, standard probability-estimation training can be retained by applying noise correction only when making predictions.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates data collection from deciding what to optimize. An agent first explores an environment without reward signals, then uses the collected trajectories to plan for subsequently supplied reward functions. This is useful when one dataset must support multiple objectives or when further interaction will be unavailable during planning.

The proposed Staged Sampling and Truncated Planning algorithm gives a bound on the exploration needed to support nearly optimal policies. Apart from logarithmic factors, the episode requirement scales with the square of the state count, the action count, and the inverse square of the target error. Its dependence on planning horizon is only logarithmic, improving on the polynomial dependence in the prior results described.

The bound matches the stated minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors. The analysis introduces a sufficient condition for a dataset to support accurate planning, an efficient soft-truncated planning method under that condition, and an extended decision process for optimizing truncated accumulated rewards. Together, these techniques connect purposeful exploration to flexible later planning.
icml-2021-near-optimal-reward-free-reinf.tldr: Staged exploration and truncated planning enable reward-free reinforcement learning with nearly optimal sample complexity and only logarithmic dependence on planning horizon.

paragraphs: This paper studies modifications to training data intended to make a neural network generalize poorly after learning from that data. The motivation is that people collecting large datasets may scrape material whose owners do not want it used for training. A generalization attack gives such owners a possible way to interfere with that use.

The attacker aims to change the training examples only slightly while disrupting the eventual training outcome. Designing those changes is difficult because it involves a bilevel optimization problem: the attack must account for how a network will learn from the modified data. The authors introduce Neural Tangent Generalization Attack, or NTGA, to address this computational obstacle.

The authors describe NTGA, to their knowledge, as the first approach enabling clean-label, black-box generalization attacks against deep networks. This means the attack preserves labels and operates in a black-box setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in the studied cases, supporting the possibility of impairing later generalization through small changes to the supplied training data.
icml-2021-neural-tangent-generalization-.tldr: NTGA slightly modifies training data while preserving labels to impair the generalization of neural networks trained on it.

paragraphs: SubgraphX explains a graph neural network's prediction by identifying important subgraphs within its input. The motivation is that individual node or edge scores can overlook meaningful graph structures. An explanation expressed as a subgraph can show a structured part of the input, making the model's apparent reasoning more intuitive to a person examining it.

Given a trained model and an input graph, the method uses Monte Carlo tree search to explore candidate subgraphs. It scores their importance using Shapley values, which account for interactions among subgraphs. This guides the search toward structures that matter for the prediction while treating their contributions in the context of other graph components.

Because computing these values can be costly, the authors develop approximation schemes specifically for graph data. The resulting procedure combines structured exploration with a practical approximation of importance. Experiments report significantly improved explanations while keeping computation at a reasonable level. The paper's central contribution is directly selecting subgraphs as explanations, supported by both a search method and an interaction-aware scoring approach.
icml-2021-on-explainability-of-graph-neu.tldr: SubgraphX explains graph neural network predictions by searching for important subgraphs and scoring their contributions with approximate Shapley values.

paragraphs: Repeated hypothesis testing creates opportunities to mistake noise for a real discovery. False discovery rate control addresses this problem while trying to preserve the ability to detect true effects. This paper adds a second requirement: the testing procedure must protect the underlying sample through differential privacy.

The focus is online testing, where each hypothesis requires an immediate decision after its test is performed. The procedure cannot wait until every test result is available before choosing which hypotheses to reject. This timing requirement distinguishes the problem from offline private testing and makes the sequence of decisions central to the algorithm's design.

The authors construct private algorithms from leading non-private online false discovery rate methods. They provide provable guarantees for privacy and for statistical performance, measured through false discovery rate and power, the ability to make correct discoveries. Experiments across several data environments demonstrate the algorithms' efficacy. The contribution brings privacy protection and statistical error control together in a setting requiring decisions as tests arrive.
icml-2021-paprika-private-online-false-d.tldr: PAPRIKA provides differentially private online hypothesis testing with guarantees for false discovery rate and statistical power.

paragraphs: Poolingformer addresses long-document modeling through two levels of attention. The first level gathers information from nearby positions using a small sliding window. The second reaches across a larger window, expanding the context available to the model. Pooling attention in that larger window reduces the associated computation and memory requirements.

The design gives nearby information and wider context distinct roles within the same attention scheme. Local aggregation supplies information from neighbors, while the larger window expands the receptive field without retaining the full cost of attention across that window. The paper evaluates whether this combination translates into stronger performance on tasks involving long inputs.

On the reported official question-answering leaderboards, Poolingformer leads on NQ long answers and both TyDi QA passage and minimal answers. The reported F1 improvements over previous leading models are 1.9, 1.9, and 1.6 points, respectively. Experiments on arXiv summarization also report superior performance, extending the evidence from finding answers in long documents to producing summaries of them.
icml-2021-poolingformer-long-document-mo.tldr: Poolingformer combines local attention with pooled attention over a larger window to model long documents efficiently and improve reported task performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops probabilistic models based on generating functions, which encode values as polynomial coefficients. The authors introduce probabilistic generating circuits, or PGCs, as an efficient way to represent these functions. Their aim is to combine tractable probabilistic modeling with a broader ability to represent distributions compactly.

The theoretical result is greater expressive efficiency than several existing tractable model families, including determinantal point processes, probabilistic circuits such as sum-product networks, and tractable graphical models. This concerns how efficiently distributions can be represented, making the contribution more than a shared notation for existing approaches. The framework also provides a way to connect previously different kinds of probabilistic models.

To investigate practical relevance, the authors construct a simple PGC class that is not trivially captured by simple combinations of probabilistic circuits and determinantal point processes. It achieves competitive performance on density-estimation benchmarks. The paper also identifies a connection to strongly Rayleigh distributions, linking the circuit framework with an established theoretical family while providing empirical evidence of modeling potential.
icml-2021-probabilistic-generating-circu.tldr: Probabilistic generating circuits use polynomial generating functions to offer greater expressive efficiency than several tractable model families and competitive density estimation.

paragraphs: Boundary-based black-box attacks seek adversarial inputs using only a model's final predictions. For high-dimensional images, the number of required queries is a central practical concern. This paper studies how that query requirement depends on the scale at which an attack operates, rather than treating the scale as an incidental design choice.

The authors develop a theoretical framework for projective gradient estimation and prove that an optimal scale exists within that framework. Their analysis also explains successful behavior of existing boundary attacks. They turn these findings into Progressive-Scale Boundary Attack, or PSBA, and use Progressive-GAN to optimize projection scale in the PSBA-PGAN variant.

Experiments examine both spatial and frequency scales across MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and ImageNet, including tests against a face-recognition API. PSBA-PGAN significantly improves query efficiency and attack success rate over the evaluated baselines. The authors also observe relatively stable optimal scales across different models and datasets. These results support scale selection as an effective component of the studied black-box attacks.
icml-2021-progressive-scale-boundary-bla.tldr: PSBA progressively adjusts projection scale to improve the query efficiency and success of boundary-based black-box attacks.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when an adaptive adversary corrupts both rewards and transitions. The adversary can alter every step within selected episodes, provided those episodes make up at most an epsilon fraction of learning. The authors describe this attack model as strictly stronger than those considered in earlier work.

They first establish an unavoidable error barrier of order epsilon. They then show that natural policy gradient retains robustness when reward corruption is bounded, with policy error of order the square root of epsilon. This result identifies an existing method's useful robustness property while making its dependence on bounded reward corruption explicit.

The proposed Filtered Policy Gradient algorithm also tolerates unbounded reward corruption and achieves error of order epsilon to the one-quarter power. Its guarantee therefore covers a broader corruption setting, though it does not match the stated lower-bound dependence. The authors emphasize its meaningful guarantee when a constant fraction of episodes is corrupted. A neural implementation also shows strong robust learning performance on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks.
icml-2021-robust-policy-gradient-against.tldr: Filtered Policy Gradient provides learning guarantees despite adversarially corrupted episodes, including cases with unbounded reward corruption.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization objectives made from three functions: one differentiable but nonconvex term, and two convex terms that may be nondifferentiable. This structure allows a smooth-looking loss component to be combined with terms expressing constraints or other nonsmooth requirements. The authors investigate how Three Operator Splitting behaves for this problem template.

Their main contribution is a convergence analysis with finite-iteration bounds on nonstationarity and infeasibility errors. These quantities describe progress toward a stationary solution and satisfaction of feasibility requirements. Unlike the existing nonconvex analyses discussed in the abstract, the guarantees do not impose additional smoothness assumptions on the objective's terms.

That distinction allows the results to cover indicator-function terms, which encode constraints, making the analysis relevant to important constrained problems. The authors also extend their guarantees to a stochastic setting where only an unbiased gradient estimator is available. Numerical experiments on quadratic assignment problems illustrate the method's effectiveness. The theoretical contribution concerns convergence behavior for this nonconvex structure, rather than a claim of finding a global optimum.
icml-2021-three-operator-splitting-with-.tldr: The paper extends Three Operator Splitting guarantees to a nonconvex loss with two convex nonsmooth terms, including constrained and stochastic settings.

paragraphs: This paper builds robustness into a neural network's basic operations. It focuses on adversarial perturbations bounded in the infinity norm, which limits the largest change to any input coordinate. The authors introduce neurons based on infinity-norm distance, aiming to support mathematical robustness guarantees rather than relying only on tests against particular attacks.

They prove that networks constructed from these neurons are 1-Lipschitz in the infinity norm: their output changes are bounded by the corresponding input changes. Combined with the margin between prediction outputs, this gives a certified robustness guarantee. They also establish that the architecture can approximate any 1-Lipschitz function and provide a robust generalization guarantee.

A dedicated training strategy alleviates optimization difficulties associated with the architecture. The reported certified accuracies are 93.09% on MNIST at perturbation radius 0.3, 35.42% on CIFAR-10 at 8/255, and 16.31% on TinyImageNet at 1/255. These results connect the architectural guarantee to trained classifiers, with each reported accuracy tied to its specified perturbation radius.
icml-2021-towards-certifying-l-infinity-.tldr: Infinity-distance neurons produce 1-Lipschitz networks whose prediction margins support certified robustness to bounded infinity-norm perturbations.

paragraphs: Deep generative models sometimes assign higher density to unfamiliar images than to images from their training distribution. This challenges their use for out-of-distribution detection. The paper investigates whether these failures arise from errors in the learned distribution or from a deeper mismatch between likelihood and the desired detection task.

The authors first prove that no detection method can guarantee better-than-chance performance without assumptions about which out-distributions matter. They then examine the typical-set hypothesis, which proposes defining detection through a distribution's typical set because relevant unfamiliar inputs may occupy high-likelihood regions. Their analysis highlights consequences of overlapping distribution supports and questions the arbitrariness of using the typical set for detection.

The results suggest that estimation error is a more plausible explanation of the observed failures than an inherent misalignment of likelihood with relevant out-distributions. The authors illustrate that even small estimation errors can cause detection failures. This redirects attention toward the accuracy of generative modeling while retaining the need to specify assumptions about the unfamiliar distributions being considered.
icml-2021-understanding-failures-in-out-.tldr: The paper argues that distribution-estimation errors more plausibly explain generative-model OOD failures than the typical-set hypothesis.

paragraphs: Standard self-attention models interactions between pairs of tokens, giving it a cost that grows quadratically with sequence length. This makes long inputs expensive. The paper proposes estimating attention through Bernoulli sampling and locality-sensitive hashing, reducing the stated complexity to linear growth with sequence length.

The key reformulation treats attention as a sum of token contributions associated with Bernoulli random variables. In principle, a single hash can sample these variables together; practical implementations may use a small constant number instead. The authors modify locality-sensitive hashing to support efficient GPU execution, connecting the sampling idea to an implementation suited to transformer training.

On GLUE with sequence length 512, the method shows favorable performance relative to a standard pretrained transformer. On Long Range Arena, its results are consistent with softmax attention while providing substantial speed and memory benefits, and it often outperforms other efficient attention methods. These findings support sampling as a practical way to reduce attention cost while retaining useful performance on the evaluated tasks.
icml-2021-you-only-sample-almost-once-li.tldr: YOSO uses hashing-based Bernoulli sampling to estimate self-attention at linear cost, with reported speed and memory gains on long sequences.
